question: A project's instructions tell Claude to "respond as our compliance officer and give final approval on vendor contracts". What is the greatest risk in writing the instructions this way?
options: A) It assigns Claude a decision role a person must own, so drafts may be treated as approvals nobody reviewed.
B) It uses a job title that Claude cannot recognise, so the instruction is skipped and the default tone applies.
C) It prevents the project knowledge base from being used, since role rules take priority over uploaded files.
D) It makes the project visible to everyone in the organisation, because role rules imply shared ownership.
correct_answers: A) It assigns Claude a decision role a person must own, so drafts may be treated as approvals nobody reviewed.
explanations: Correct. Framing durable direction as decision authority invites colleagues to treat output as a sign-off.
Role framing is understood; the danger is the authority it implies, not a failure to parse the title.
Instructions and uploaded knowledge work together; one does not switch the other off.
Instruction wording has no effect on who the project is shared with.
